verses.zh: 以利户又接着说：
verses.en: Elihu said further:[NOTE:1]
notes: This very lengthy speech can be broken down into the following sections: the discipline of suffering (36:2-25), the work and wisdom of God (36:26-37:24).

verses.zh: 你再容我片时，我就指示你，因我还有话为　神说。
verses.en: “Be patient[NOTE:1] with me a little longer,and I will instruct you,for I still have words to speak on God’s behalf.[NOTE:2]
notes: The use of וַיֹּסֶף (vayyosef) is with the hendiadys construction: “and he added and said,” meaning “and he said again, further.”

The verb כָּתַּר (kattar) is the Piel imperative; in Hebrew the word means “to surround” and is related to the noun for crown. But in Syriac it means “to wait.” This section of the book of Job will have a few Aramaic words.
verses.commentary:
36:2 "Wait for me a little while"
This is a Piel IMPERATIVE
(BDB 509, KB 506). The Hebrew root normally means "to surround"
but in Syrian it means "to wait."

▣ "I will show you"
This is a Piel IMPERFECT
(BDB 296, KB 295) used in a COHORTATIVE
sense.

This verse is a literary way for Elihu to express his desire that Job hear
him (cf. Job 33:1b; 34:2,10,16; 37:14). Elihu is arrogantly asserting
he, and he alone, really has true wisdom (cf. Job 36:4b; 33:3-4) and is
speaking for God!

36:3a This may be idiomatic for
Elihu gathering information about God from

- a variety of places

- God Himself (see same word used in Ps. 139:2)

Therefore, it becomes an assertion of his complete and full knowledge of
God.

36:3b Elihu asserts that he can
substantiate that God is just and fair, which Job has denied.

▣ "my Maker" The
MT (BDB 821, KB 950, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)
asserts God as creator of human beings (i.e. Genesis 2). A synonymous
title was used in Job 35:10 (BDB 793 I, KB 889, Qal
ACTIVE PARTICIPLE).

36:4a This implies that Job's
words, also as well as his three comforters' words, are false! Only
Elihu has true and complete knowledge of God (Job 36:4b). He claims a
unique illumination in Job 33:3.

verses.zh: 我要将所知道的从远处引来，将公义归给造我的主。
verses.en: With my knowledge I will speak comprehensively,[NOTE:1] and to my Creator I will ascribe righteousness.[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew text simply has “for yet for God words.”
Heb “I will carry my knowledge to-from afar.” The expression means that he will give a wide range to knowledge, that he will speak comprehensively.

verses.zh: 我的言语真不虚谎；有知识全备的与你同在。
verses.en: For in truth, my words are not false;it is one complete[NOTE:1] in knowledge who is with you.
notes: This line gives the essence of all of Elihu’s speech—to give or ascribe righteousness to God against the charges of Job. Dhorme translates this “I will justify my Maker,” and that is workable if it carries the meaning of “declaring to be right.”

verses.zh: 神有大能，并不藐视人；他的智慧甚广。
verses.en: Indeed, God is mighty, and he does not despise people;[NOTE:1] he[NOTE:2] is mighty, and firm[NOTE:3] in his intent.[NOTE:4]
notes: The word is תְּמִים (temim), often translated “perfect.” It is the same word used of Job in 2:3. Elihu is either a complete stranger to modesty or is confident regarding the knowledge that he believes God has revealed to him for this situation. See the note on the heading before 32:1.
The object “people” is not in the Hebrew text but is implied.
The text simply repeats “mighty.”
The last two words are simply כֹּחַ לֵב (koakh lev, “strong in heart”), meaning something like “strong; firm in his decisions.”
verses.commentary:
36:5-16 Here is a list of the actions of God.

- God is mighty, Job 36:5a

- God despises no one, Job 36:5a

- God is mighty in understanding (lit. heart), Job 36:5b

- God destroys the wicked, Job 36:6a; kings also, Job 36:12-16

- God gives justice to the afflicted, Job 36:6b

- God does not withdraw His eyes from the righteous, Job 36:7a

- God places kings on their thrones, Job 36:7b

- God instructs kings, Job 36:10a

- God commands they repent of evil, Job 36:8-10

- God blesses obedient, repentant kings, Job 36:11

Though Elihu uses "kings," he is obviously referring to Job as
a tribal elder or community elder (cf. Job 36:17-23).

36:5b "understanding"
This is literally "heart." NJB accepts an emendation and
reads, "whose heart is pure." The UBS Text Project (p. 123)
gives the NASB translation of the MT a "B" rating (some
doubt).

The theological essence of this line of poetry is that God acts on His
purposes and is resolute in accomplishing them.

36:6a This is the theology of
"the two ways" (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; 30:15,19;
Psalm 1). Job has disagreed with this (cf. Job 9:24;
21:7). As Job is an exception, so too, the prosperous wicked!

verses.zh: 他不保护恶人的性命，却为困苦人伸冤。
verses.en: He does not allow the wicked to live,[NOTE:1] but he gives justice to the poor.
notes: There are several problems in this verse: the repetition of “mighty,” the lack of an object for “despise,” and the meaning of “strength of heart.” Many commentators reduce the verse to a single line, reading something like “Lo, God does not reject the pure in heart” (Kissane). Dhorme and Pope follow Nichols with: “Lo, God is mighty in strength, and rejects not the pure in heart.” This reading moved “mighty” to the first line and took the second to be בַּר (bar, “pure”).

verses.zh: 他时常看顾义人，使他们和君王同坐宝座，永远要被高举。
verses.en: He does not take his eyes[NOTE:1] off the righteous;but with kings on the throne he seats the righteous[NOTE:2] and exalts them forever.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “he does not keep the wicked alive.”
Many commentators accept the change of “his eyes” to “his right” (reading דִּינוֹ [dino] for עֵינָיו [ʿenayv]). There is no compelling reason for the change; it makes the line commonplace.
Heb “them”; the referent (the righteous) has been repeated from the first part of the verse for clarity.
verses.commentary:
36:7 The interpretive issue becomes, "Are there two
groups in Job 36:7 or just one?"

- the righteous

- kings

"Kings" seems out of place unless it is an allusion to

- Job's tribal/area leadership

- imagery of the righteous being treated as a king

verses.zh: 他们若被锁链捆住，被苦难的绳索缠住，
verses.en: But if they are bound in chains[NOTE:1] and held captive by the cords of affliction,
notes: Heb “he seats them forever and exalts them.” The last verb can be understood as expressing a logical consequence of the preceding action (cf. GKC 328 §111.l = “he seats them forever so that he exalts them”). Or the two verbs can be taken as an adverbial hendiadys whereby the first modifies the second adverbially: “he exalts them by seating them forever” or “when he seats them forever” (cf. GKC 326 §111.d). Some interpret this verse to say that God seats kings on the throne, making a change in subject in the middle of the verse. But it makes better sense to see the righteous as the subject matter throughout—they are not only protected, but are exalted.
verses.commentary:
36:8-11 Elihu asserts that the
purpose of suffering may be to help turn back to God a faithful follower
who has sinned (Job 36:15). This is the stated purpose of the "cursing"
passages in the Mosaic Covenant (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-30).

36:8 The concept of being bound
by God (cf. Job 36:13) is a Hebrew idiom for judgment (i.e., Ps. 107:10;
149:8). The opposite idiom is "to set free" (cf. Ps. 146:7;
Isa. 42:7; 49:9; 61:1).

verses.zh: 他就把他们的作为和过犯指示他们，叫他们知道有骄傲的行动。
verses.en: then he reveals[NOTE:1] to them what they have done[NOTE:2] and their transgressions, that they were behaving proudly.
notes: Dhorme thinks that the verse is still talking about kings, who may be in captivity. But this diverts attention from Elihu’s emphasis on the righteous.
The verb נָגַד (nagad) means “to declare; to tell.” Here it is clear that God is making known the sins that caused the enslavement or captivity, so “reveal” makes a good interpretive translation.

verses.zh: 他也开通他们的耳朵得受教训，吩咐他们离开罪孽转回。
verses.en: And he reveals[NOTE:1] this[NOTE:2] for correctionand says that they must turn[NOTE:3] from evil.
notes: Heb “their work.”
The idiom once again is “he uncovers their ear.”
The revelation is in the preceding verse, and so a pronoun must be added to make the reference clear.
verses.commentary:
36:10 "He opens their ear to instruction" This is a
Hebrew idiom. God initiates revelation (cf. Job 33:16; 36:15); mankind
can only respond to God's initiation. This is covenant (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT).

Literally, the VERB is
"uncovers" (BDB 162, KB 191, Qal
IMPERFECT with waw, cf. Zech. 7:11). This
is similar to the idiom of "circumcise your ears" (i.e., Jer.
6:10; Acts 7:51).

▣ "return from evil"
This VERB (BDB 996, KB
1427, Qal IMPERFECT)
is one of several Hebrew terms which denotes a change of spiritual
direction. See SPECIAL
TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT).

Notice in Job 36:10 how the sovereign God reveals His will but calls on
a human person to respond. This is the intersection of election and free
will. Both are biblical; both are true; both are necessary.

SPECIAL
TOPIC: ELECTION/PREDESTINATION AND THE NEED FOR A THEOLOGICAL BALANCE

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

verses.zh: 他们若听从事奉他，就必度日亨通，历年福乐；
verses.en: If they obey and serve him,they live out their days in prosperityand their years in pleasantness.[NOTE:1]
notes: The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “to turn; to return”) is one of the two major words in the OT for “repent”—to return from evil. Here the imperfect should be obligatory—they must do it.
verses.commentary:
36:11-12 "If they hear and serve"
This is the essence of the VERB
shema (cf. Deut. 6:4-6), "to hear, so as to do" (cf.
James 1:22-25).

Notice the traditional "two ways" emphasis—repent and be
prosperous and live a long life.

36:12a

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, NIV
"perish by the sword"

TEV
"cross the stream"

NJB
"go down the canal"

REB
"cross the river of death"

NET
"pass over the river of death"

Peshitta
"perish by destruction"

The Hebrew VERB (BDB 716,
KB 778) means "to pass over" or "to pass through."
It has a wide semantic field. However, it is often used in connection
with

- death involving water – Ps. 88:16-17; 124:3-4; Jonah 2:4; Isa. 54:9

- death – Job 33:18; 34:20; Ps. 37:36

However, the word "sword" (BDB 1019, cf. Job 15:22) gives the
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA textual support for their translation, "perish."

verses.zh: 若不听从，就要被刀杀灭，无知无识而死。
verses.en: But if they refuse to listen,they pass over the river of death[NOTE:1] and expire without knowledge.
notes: Some commentators delete this last line for metrical considerations. But there is no textual evidence for the deletion; it is simply the attempt by some to make the meter rigid.

verses.zh: 那心中不敬虔的人积蓄怒气；　神捆绑他们，他们竟不求救；
verses.en: The godless at heart[NOTE:1] nourish anger;[NOTE:2] they do not cry out even when he binds them.
notes: This is a similar expression to the one in Job 33:18, where the suggestion was made by many that it means crossing over the canal or river of death. Some retain the earlier interpretation of “perish by the sword” (cf. NIV).
The expression “godless [or hypocrite] in heart” is an intensification of the description. It conveys that they are intentionally godless. See Matt 23:28.
verses.commentary:
36:13 When the godless do not call out to God ("binds" them), but when
the faithful do (God "delivers" them, cf. Job 36:15). The VERB
in v. 13b is "He binds them" (BDB 63, KB 75, Qal PERFECT).
The VERB "delivers" (BDB 322 I, KB 321, Piel
IMPERFECT) in Job 36:15 denotes God saving/delivering

- from affliction, Job 36:15; Ps. 119:153

- from calamity, Ps. 18:18-19

- from trouble, Ps. 34:6-7; 50:15; 81:7; 91:15

- from death, Ps. 56:13; 116:8

36:14b

NASB
"among cult prostitutes"

NKJV
"among the perverted persons"

NRSV
"in shame"

TEV
"disgrace"

NJB
"among the male prostitutes of the temple"

JPSOA
"the depraved"

REB
"male prostitutes"

LXX
"my messengers" (angels)

Peshitta
"snatched by famine"

NET
"male cultic prostitutes"

The MT has "temple prostitute" (male, cf. Deut. 23:17; 1 Kgs.
14:24; 15:12; 22:46; 2 Kgs. 23:7). The FEMININE form is
used in Deut. 23:17; Hos. 4:14. It is used of harlotry in general in Gen. 38:21-22.

Temple prostitutes are associated with fertility worship (i.e.,
imitation magic). Exactly how Job would have known of this is uncertain.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

verses.zh: 必在青年时死亡，与污秽人一样丧命。
verses.en: They die[NOTE:1] in their youth,and their life ends among the male cultic prostitutes.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “they put anger.” This is usually interpreted to mean they lay up anger, or put anger in their hearts.
The text expresses this with “their soul dies.”

verses.zh: 神藉着困苦救拔困苦人，趁他们受欺压开通他们的耳朵。
verses.en: He delivers the afflicted by[NOTE:1] their[NOTE:2] afflictions;he reveals himself to them[NOTE:3] by their suffering.
notes: Heb “among the male prostitutes” who were at the temple—the “holy ones,” with “holy” being used in that sense of “separated to that form of temple service.” So uncleanness and shame are some of the connotations of the reference. Some modern translations give the general sense only: “their life ends in shame” (NRSV); “and perish among the reprobate” (NAB); “die…after wasting their lives in immoral living” (NLT).

The preposition ב (bet) in these two lines is not location but instrument, not “in” but “by means of.” The affliction and the oppression serve as a warning for sin, and therefore a means of salvation.
Heb “his.”
verses.commentary:
36:15-16 This is the key thought
in the dialogues (Job 4-37). God delivers the afflicted who turn to Him.
The new thought is that "affliction" itself is a tool to help
sinners turn back to God (cf. Heb. 12:5-13).

verses.zh: 神也必引你出离患难，进入宽阔不狭窄之地；摆在你席上的必满有肥甘。
verses.en: And surely, he drew you[NOTE:1] from the mouth of distress,to a wide place, unrestricted,[NOTE:2] and to the comfort[NOTE:3] of your tablefilled with rich food.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “he uncovers their ear.”

The Hebrew verb means “to entice; to lure; to allure; to seduce,” but these have negative connotations. The English “to persuade; to draw” might work better. The verb is the Hiphil perfect of סוּת (sut). But the nuance of the verb is difficult. It can be equivalent to an English present expressing what God is doing (Peake). But the subject is contested as well. Since the verb usually has an evil connotation, there have been attempts to make the “plaza” the subject—“the wide place has led you astray” (Ewald).
Heb “a broad place where there is no cramping beneath [or under] it.”

The word נַחַת (nakhat) could be translated “set” if it is connected with the verb נוּחַ (nuakh, “to rest,” but then “to lay to rest, to set”). Kissane translates it “comfort.” Dhorme thinks it could come from נוּחַ (nuakh, “to rest”) or נָחַת (nakhat, “to descend”). But his conclusion is that it is a dittography after “under it” (p. 545).
verses.commentary:
36:16-20 Notice the statements of scholars.

- The AB (p. 233) says, "These verses are so difficult that
many critics omit them in despair."

- The UBS Handbook (p. 665) says "Job 36:16-21 are extremely
difficult to interpret and as Rowley says, ‘scarcely any two interpreters
are agreed as to their meanings.'"

- NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 786, says, "It is uncertain whether Job is being
accused, warned, or encouraged. It is also unclear by what means the
sufferer is being (NIV), or was (RSV), or will be (Dhorme, 544-45) enticed. . ."

36:16a "from the mouth of distress"
What powerful personification imagery!

36:16b,c These two lines of poetry draw on two Hebrew idioms.

- "a broad place" – this is the opposite of a tight,
restricted place (i.e., trouble, pain, doubt, fear, etc); it comes from
penned up animals being released into pasture (i.e., freedom from
restrictions). The NOUN (BDB 931) occurs only here.

- "table full of fatness" – this is imagery for
wonderful, boundless food (opposite of hunger and need)

36:16 is contrasted with the fullness of judgment. Elihu is accusing Job
of improper use of his wealth, influence, and position (i.e., Job
36:19).

The other option is a warning not to think too highly of your case
(i.e., Job's legal case, cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 305) against God or the
"ransom" (Job 33:24, which refers to the work of the angelic
advocate).

verses.zh: 但你满口有恶人批评的言语；判断和刑罚抓住你。
verses.en: But now you are preoccupied with the judgment due the wicked;judgment and justice take hold of you.
verses.commentary:
36:17 I am not sure the NASB
paragraphing is accurate here. It seems the fullness of plenty in Job

verses.zh: 不可容忿怒触动你，使你不服责罚；也不可因赎价大就偏行。
verses.en: Be careful that[NOTE:1] no one entices you with riches;do not let a large bribe[NOTE:2] turn you aside.
notes: Heb “filled with fat.”
The first expression is idiomatic: the text says, “because wrath lest it entice you”—thus, beware.
verses.commentary:
36:18 Job 36:18 could be

- an IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
(NASB, "let. . .")

- just another IMPERFECT (this chapter has many)

The word NASB translates as "ransom" (BDB 49) can also mean
"bribe" (i.e., 1 Sam. 12:3; Pro. 6:35; Amos 5:12).

verses.zh: 你的呼求（或译：资财），或是你一切的势力，果有灵验，叫你不受患难吗？
verses.en: Would your wealth[NOTE:1] sustain you,so that you would not be in distress,[NOTE:2] even all your mighty efforts?[NOTE:3]
notes: The word is כֹּפֶר (kofer), often translated “ransom,” but frequently in the sense of a bribe.
The form in the MT is “your cry (for help).” See J. E. Hartley (Job [NICOT], 472-73) and E. Dhorme (Job, 547-48) on the difficulties.
This part has only two words לֹא בְצָר (loʾ betsar, “not in distress”). The negated phrase serves to explain the first colon.
verses.commentary:
36:19 The NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p.
441, says the phrase, "the forces of your strength," is
impossible to translate. There have been numerous suggestions. They
assert Job 36:19 is a "virtually unintelligible text."

verses.zh: 不要切慕黑夜，就是众民在本处被除灭的时候。
verses.en: Do not long for the cover of nightto drag people away from their homes.[NOTE:1]
notes: For the many suggestions and the reasoning here, see the commentaries.
verses.commentary:
36:20 This is another difficult
verse; possibly evil doers seek the night for their evil acts.

36:21a This is a Niphal IMPERATIVE
("take heed," BDB 1036, KB 1581) followed by a negated Qal
JUSSIVE ("do not turn," BDB 815, KB 937).

verses.zh: 你要谨慎，不可重看罪孽，因你选择罪孽过于选择苦难。
verses.en: Take heed; do not turn to evil,for because of this you have been tested[NOTE:1] by affliction.
notes: The meaning of this line is difficult. There are numerous suggestions for emending the text. Kissane takes the first verb in the sense of “oppress,” and for “the night” he has “belonging to you,” meaning “your people.” This reads: “Oppress not them that belong not to you, that your kinsmen may mount up in their place.”

verses.zh: 神行事有高大的能力；教训人的有谁像他呢？
verses.en: Indeed, God is exalted in his power;who is a teacher[NOTE:1] like him?
notes: Normally “tested” would be the translation for the Niphal of בָּחַר (bakhar). Although the Qal is employed here, the context favors “tested” rather than “chose.”
verses.commentary:
36:22-23 Again, Elihu lists God's
characteristics (cf. Job 36:5-16).

- God is exalted in His power (i.e., men see it in creation, Job 36:25a)

- God is an unmatched teacher (i.e., true wisdom)

- God is sovereign, Job 36:23

This emphasis on the sovereign power of the creator God foreshadows
God's response to Job in Job 38-41.

verses.zh: 谁派定他的道路？谁能说：你所行的不义？
verses.en: Who has prescribed his ways for him?Or said to him, ‘You have done what is wicked’?

verses.zh: 你不可忘记称赞他所行的为大，就是人所歌颂的。
verses.en: Remember to extol[NOTE:1] his work,which people have praised in song.
notes: The word מוֹרֶה (moreh) is the Hiphil participle from יָרַה (yarah). It is related to the noun תּוֹרָה (torah, “what is taught” i.e., the law).
verses.commentary:
36:24-33 These verses describe
God as creator with imagery from nature (esp. water; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS). Water was seen as a blessing from God. The regular
cycles of nature were seen in a divine activity (i.e., Divine Sustainer).

The context of this strophe continues into the next chapter and
introduces the words of God in Job 38-41. God is the sovereign Lord of
all created things (animate and inanimate).

36:26a This is not an affirmation
of the unknowability of God (i.e., Ecclesiastes) but a Hebrew idiom
expressing that humans cannot fully comprehend the greatness of God (cf.
Job 5:9; 11:7).

36:27b

NASB, NKJV, NJB, JPSOA
"the mist"

TEV, Peshitta
"drops of rain"

REB
"the flood"

LXX
"into a cloud"

The MT has the NOUN "mist"
(BDB 15, KB 11) that occurs only twice in the OT, Gen. 2:6 and here. KB
suggests several options.

- sea-foam (Targums)

- inundation of floods (Akkadian)

- subterranean stream of fresh water (i.e., Sumerian, cf. Gen. 2:6)

- celestial stream (Arabic)

The word here seems to refer to atmospheric water (rain). The three
sources of agricultural water were

- irrigation/annual flooding

- rain (mostly in storms)

- dew

verses.zh: 他所行的，万人都看见；世人也从远处观看。
verses.en: All humanity has seen it;people gaze on it from afar.

verses.zh: 神为大，我们不能全知；他的年数不能测度。
verses.en: “Yes, God is great—beyond our knowledge![NOTE:1] The number of his years is unsearchable.
notes: The expression is “that you extol,” serving as an object of the verb.

verses.zh: 他吸取水点，这水点从云雾中就变成雨；
verses.en: He draws up drops of water;they distill[NOTE:1] the rain into its mist,[NOTE:2]
notes: The last part has the verbal construction, “and we do not know.” This clause is to be used adverbially: “beyond our understanding.”
The verb means “to filter; to refine,” and so a plural subject with the drops of water as the subject will not work. So many read the singular, “he distills.”

verses.zh: 云彩将雨落下，沛然降与世人。
verses.en: which the clouds pour downand shower on humankind abundantly.
verses.commentary:
36:28 "They drip upon man"
There are several places where "adam" ("mankind,"
BDB 9 IV) can be parallel to "erets" (i.e., land,
ground, cf. Pro. 30:14; Jer. 32:20; Zech. 13:5). This translation makes
Job 36:28 make more sense (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 263, 267).

36:30b

NASB, NKJV, TEV
"depths of the sea"

NRSV, LXX
"roots of the sea"

NJB
"the tops of the mountains"

JPSOA, Peshsitta
"the bed of the sea"

REB
"the sea"

The MT has the NOUN CONSTRUCT,
"the roots (BDB 1057) of the sea" (BDB 410). The NJB fits the
parallelism best, but "roots" may be another allusion to the
ancient subterranean pillars (cf. Job 9:6; 28:9; 38:4,6; 1 Sam. 2:8; Ps.
75:3; 104:5) that support the earth amidst the cosmic chaotic waters
(cf. Gen. 1:2; Ps. 24:2; 104:3).

verses.zh: 谁能明白云彩如何铺张，和　神行宫的雷声呢？
verses.en: Who can understand the spreading of the clouds,the thunderings of his pavilion?[NOTE:1]
notes: This word עֵד (ʿed) occurs also in Gen 2:6. The suggestion has been that instead of a mist it represents an underground watercourse that wells up to water the ground.

verses.zh: 他将亮光普照在自己的四围；他又遮覆海底。
verses.en: See how he scattered[NOTE:1] his lightning[NOTE:2] about him;he has covered the depths[NOTE:3] of the sea.
notes: Heb “his booth.”
The word actually means “to spread,” but with lightning as the object, “to scatter” appears to fit the context better.
The word is “light,” but taken to mean “lightning.” Theodotion had “mist” here, and so most commentators follow that because it is more appropriate to the verb and the context.

verses.zh: 他用这些审判众民，且赐丰富的粮食。
verses.en: It is by these that he judges[NOTE:1] the nationsand supplies food in abundance.
notes: Heb “roots.”
verses.commentary:
36:31 "He judges peoples"
This phrase reflects God's universal control (cf. Job 37:12c; Ps. 9:8;
96:10). The use of "El," the general name for deity in
the ANE, reflects this connotation. He is God of all!

The NJB, NAB, and REB translations emend "to judge" (BDB 192,
KB 220, Qal imperfect)
to "to nourish/supply" in order to make lines a and b more
parallel (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 1089; NET Bible, p. 839)

verses.zh: 他以电光遮手，命闪电击中敌人（或译：中了靶子）。
verses.en: With his hands[NOTE:1] he covers[NOTE:2] the lightningand directs it against its target.
notes: The verb is יָדִין (yadin, “he judges”). Houbigant proposed יָזוּן (yazun, “he nourishes”). This has found wide acceptance among commentators (cf. NAB). G. R. Driver retained the MT but gave a meaning “enriches” to the verb (“Problems in the Hebrew text of Job,” VTSup 3 [1955]: 88ff.).
R. Gordis (Job, 422) prefers to link this word with the later Hebrew word for “arch,” not “hands.”

verses.zh: 所发的雷声显明他的作为，又向牲畜指明要起暴风。
verses.en: [NOTE:1] His thunder announces the coming storm,the cattle also, concerning the storm’s approach.[NOTE:2]
notes: Because the image might mean that God grabs the lightning and hurls it like a javelin (cf. NLT), some commentators want to change “covers” to other verbs. Dhorme has “lifts” (נִשָּׂא [nissaʾ] for כִּסָּה [kissah]). This fit the idea of God directing the lightning bolts.

Peake knew of over thirty interpretations for this verse. The MT literally says, “He declares his purpose [or his shout] concerning it; cattle also concerning what rises.” Dhorme has it: “The flock which sniffs the coming storm has warned the shepherd.” Kissane: “The thunder declares concerning him, as he excites wrath against iniquity.” Gordis translates it: “His thunderclap proclaims his presence, and the storm his mighty wrath.” Many more could be added to the list.
verses.commentary:
36:33 "noises" This
(BDB 929) refers to the thunder of a rain storm (cf. Job 37:2).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Does Job 36:3-4 imply Elihu is claiming a special knowledge from God?

- How does Job 36:6-11 express the traditional theology of "the two ways"?

- How is the word "kings" used in Job 36:7?

- How does Job 36:10 relate to both God's sovereignty and human free will?

- Why does the word "cult prostitutes" appear in Job 36:14?

- What "ransom" does Job 36:18 refer to?

- What does "we do not know Him" in Job 36:26 mean?
